meta.name: Agentic Software Modernization — Advanced
meta.description: Advanced course building on the core Agentic Software Modernization curriculum. Covers advanced patterns, anti-patterns, retrieval and context infrastructure, and workflow and operational scaling — topics not needed in every modernization effort, but important for larger initiatives or when establishing agentic operations at scale. Assumes familiarity with the core curriculum.

levels.label: Can Apply
levels.description: Able to apply, evaluate, and adapt autonomously in real modernization situations

levels.label: Understand
levels.description: Able to explain relationships, mechanics, and tradeoffs

levels.label: Know
levels.description: Able to name and place terms and concepts in context

goals.title: Recognize and name vibe coding as an anti-pattern
goals.description: The unplanned "something-with-agents" approach that feels good and scales poorly. You need to be able to name it in order to push back — especially in teams just starting out with agents.
topics: Symptom: "just do it" prompts without acceptance criteria
goals.example: "Just modernize the backend." The agent changes imports, installs packages, writes new files. After two hours nothing runs and nobody can tell what happened. The answer is not "better agent" but disciplined task definition.

goals.title: Use the horseshoe model as an orientation framework
goals.description: Visual orientation between pure refactoring and complete rewrite. Helps in strategic discussions that without this model derail into "refactoring vs. rebuild".
topics: Abstraction level as a third dimension
goals.example: Team discusses: "Refactoring is not enough, but a rewrite is too risky." The horseshoe model shows: move up one level (extract the domain model), restructure there, then go back down to code. That is re-architecting — between the two extremes.

goals.title: Structure a modernization handbook as the leading artifact
goals.description: The document in which a modernization initiative records its strategic decisions. Distinguished from the runbook (operational guidance for day-to-day runs) and the spec (technical acceptance criteria per task).
topics: Strategy choice with rationale against rejected alternatives
goals.example: A 10-page document with target vision, scope, strategy (with rationale against alternatives), milestones, risks, and ADRs. Consulted at every steering committee meeting. The runbook and spec are separate artifacts with different scope.

goals.title: Distinguish clean-room reimplementation from a classic rewrite
goals.description: Clean-room is a deliberate, regulated variant of the rewrite — not the classic "just write it again". The distinction matters because clean-room carries its own risks.
topics: Clean-room: specification, strictly not looking at the original
Classic rewrite: done with reference to the old code
goals.example: Team reimplements a parser in clean-room style without reading the original code. Advantage: no IP risks, clear spec. Disadvantage: 17 edge cases the original handled correctly are not documented — they are lost. A classic rewrite would have carried them over.

goals.title: Distinguish idiomatic transpilation from a mere language switch
goals.description: A language switch alone is not modernization. Idiomatic means the target language is actually used in the target-language way — streams, Optional, exception hierarchies instead of a 1:1 translation.
topics: Idiomatic transpilation (patterns and idioms of the target language)
Role of agents in both variants
goals.example: COBOL function translated directly to Java: 1000 lines, no exceptions, no collections. Idiomatic version: 200 lines, streams, Optional, clean exception hierarchy. The difference determines whether the result is maintainable or merely formally translated.

goals.title: Identify dark code and neutralize it before agent work
goals.description: Code that exists but is not used or not understood. Doubly dangerous because it misleads agents: they find patterns in it and reproduce them.
topics: Detection via call graph and coverage
Marking or removal before agent deployment
goals.example: An 800-line module `LegacyMigrationHelper` is part of the build but has not been called in 4 years. The agent finds patterns in it and reproduces them — with toxic consequences. Dark code must be identified, marked, or removed before agentic work begins.

goals.title: Anchor drift detection in CI
goals.description: Where does the new version deviate from legacy behavior? Captured automatically before a human reviews — the equivalent of a golden master, but running continuously in the pipeline.
topics: Output diff against a frozen baseline snapshot
Schema drift detection for APIs and data contracts
Automated integration in CI — break on deviation, not just on test failure
goals.example: After every agent commit a diff check runs against a baseline of 500 representative calls. Deviations greater than 1% break the build. Agents are not blocked, but the system automatically catches unexpected behavior changes.

goals.title: Separate context engineering from prompt engineering
goals.description: Two related but distinct disciplines. Context engineering is strategic (lifecycle, selection); prompt engineering is tactical (wording). Conflating them means optimizing the wrong lever.
topics: Prompt: wording of a single instruction
Context: selection, maintenance, lifecycle of context building blocks
Common mistake: prompt tuning where a context strategy is missing
goals.example: Prompt engineering: "Phrase the task so it is unambiguous." Context engineering: "Which artifacts do all agents of this type need, which are loaded per session, which expire after a week?" Without the second, the first becomes squirrel optimization.

goals.title: Place MCP as a tool-connectivity standard
goals.description: The Model Context Protocol standardizes how agents communicate with tools. It reduces integration effort, increases reusability, and shifts governance to a central point.
topics: MCP as a protocol, not a tool
Governance effect: logs, limits, permissions centralized
goals.example: Three different agents need access to the internal documentation API. Without MCP: three integrations. With MCP: one server, three clients. Side effect: the server becomes the accountability point — logs, rate limits, and permissions in one place instead of three codebases.

goals.title: Apply RAG and embeddings purposefully for modernization
goals.description: Pull relevant context on demand rather than keeping it permanently in the context window. Powerful — but for code, vector similarity is no substitute for structural retrieval via call graphs.
topics: Limits with code: structure beats similarity
goals.example: 50,000 files of legacy code. RAG fetches the relevant 20 chunks per query. That works — but for code, structure is often more important than similarity, so it is supplemented by call-graph retrieval. Vectors alone rarely suffice for code.

goals.title: Design a retrieval architecture for a modernization initiative
goals.description: The transfer: how do agents in a real initiative get the information they need — and nothing beyond that.
topics: Selecting retrieval mechanisms by task type
Interplay of vector, graph, and full-text
goals.example: Migration initiative with 40 services. Decision: full-text via `ripgrep` for known symbols, embeddings for domain search, call-graph retrieval for refactoring tasks. All three behind one MCP server, logs centralized. Metric: share of agent tasks satisfied by the first retrieval response.

goals.title: Apply harness engineering and intent engineering as distinct disciplines
goals.description: Two complementary disciplines: harness builds the cage, intent formulates the assignment. Conflating them leads to misdiagnosed failures and fixes at the wrong end.
topics: Harness: tools, scripts, guardrails, feedback infrastructure
Intent: task formulation, scope, acceptance criteria
goals.example: Agent fails. Harness problem: the test run fails before the agent gets any feedback at all. Intent problem: the task was "make it better" — without a criterion every solution is correct and none is acceptable. Two different failures, two different fixes. The order: make the harness solid first, then sharpen the intent.

goals.title: Use commands, skills, and hooks as automation building blocks
goals.description: Reusable building blocks for agent work — the equivalent of libraries in classical programming. Without these mechanisms everyone reinvents everything.
goals.example: Team establishes skill `add-migration` with a fixed sequence (adjust schema, generate migration, run tests, update docs). Every agent on the team can call it — quality becomes reproducible. Without these mechanisms everyone builds their own half-baked workflow.

goals.title: Distinguish single agent, subagent, and agent team
goals.description: Three scaling levels with different coordination costs. Conflating them leads to unnecessary complexity or overloaded single agents.
topics: Coordination cost as a decision criterion
goals.example: Increasing test coverage — a single agent is enough. Modernizing a complete module — several subagents (analysis, refactoring, test augmentation) under one coordinator. A team with independent roles only pays off when coordination itself becomes the bottleneck.

goals.title: Tell apart workflow framework, orchestration, and runbook
goals.description: Three artifact classes with different scope: the framework defines the solution space, orchestration chains steps together, the runbook guides the operational run. Three audiences, three lifecycles.
topics: Runbook: operational instructions for the operator
Distinction from modernization handbook and spec
goals.example: Framework specifies: every agent has a human-in-the-loop checkpoint after tool call X. Orchestration for nightly refactoring: agent A → B → C with checks in between. Runbook for the operator: "If orchestration fails 3 times, follow escalation path D." Three artifacts, three audiences.

goals.title: Place the dark factory as a target vision and name its limits
goals.description: Fully automated work pipelines as a vision. Realistic for certain modernization types (replatform, dependency bumps), unrealistic for judgment work (re-architect, domain decisions).
goals.example: The dark factory works for upgrading 1,000 dependencies to a new major version. It does not work for reorganizing a domain. Applying the metaphor to all modernization tasks builds invisible debt in the name of automation.

goals.title: Justify the autonomy-control balance situationally
goals.description: The reasoning behind the balance, not just the design of a specific framework. Where core lesson 6 asks 'how tight should this control framework be for this task', this goal asks 'why does the right answer change — and how do you develop the judgment to know when to shift it'.
goals.example: Experienced team, repeated task, good tests: more autonomy pays off. New team, unfamiliar codebase, weak tests: autonomy is expensive. The balance shifts — less autonomy today, more in 6 months once structures and monitoring are in place.

goals.title: Design an entry-level architecture for recurring agentic modernization tasks
goals.description: The organizational transfer: how does an organization move agentic modernization from isolated experiments into regular operations without over-building.
topics: Minimal set of commands and skills
goals.example: Start with 3 skills (`add-tests`, `bump-dependency`, `extract-module`), 1 MCP server (repository access), centralized logging, and a clear human-in-the-loop rule. After 3 months assess what worked and expand from there — do not over-dimension upfront. The first architecture must hold, not shine.
